Yet much of what happens to a pupil placed in a lower group depends on what the school then does with that group: whether it is given the most experienced teachers or the least, a demanding curriculum or a diluted one, and whether pupils can move up when they improve. A lower set taught ambitiously and kept open differs more from a lower set treated as a holding pen than either does from a mixed class. Asking whether grouping works is therefore a less useful question than asking what it is used to do.

items.paragraph: Batteries are often presented as the answer to the intermittency of wind and solar power: store the surplus when the sun shines and release it when it does not. For smoothing variation over hours they are increasingly effective, absorbing the midday peak of solar output and covering the evening rise in demand. But the harder problem of intermittency is not the daily cycle. It is the windless, overcast week in winter, or the season in which output stays low for months, and covering gaps of that length with batteries of the kind now installed would require storage on a scale that is, at present, very costly. Batteries, then, solve one part of the problem well, and success with that part should not be mistaken for a solution to the whole, which will also need other means such as long-distance transmission, flexible demand or different forms of storage.

items.paragraph: Screening programmes are usually judged by how many cases of disease they find, and by that measure more sensitive tests always look better. But some conditions that screening detects would never have caused harm in a person's lifetime: small, slow-growing abnormalities that would have stayed silent until the person died of something else. Finding these is not a benefit; it converts healthy people into patients, exposing them to anxiety and to treatments with real side effects. Because no one can tell, in an individual case, whether a detected abnormality would have progressed, the overdiagnosed patient is indistinguishable from one whose life was saved, and may well believe that screening saved them. Counting detections therefore overstates what screening achieves, without implying that screening is never worthwhile.

items.paragraph: It is tempting to think of the rules of a game as fences around an activity that exists without them, but moving a bishop diagonally is not a restriction on some freer way of moving a carved piece; outside the rules there is no bishop to move. Rules in this sense constitute a game rather than regulate it. From this some infer that whatever the rules permit is fair, and that a player who finds a loophole has simply played well. The inference is too quick. Rules are written to make a particular contest possible, and a move that satisfies their letter while dissolving that contest, such as a team deliberately losing to secure an easier opponent later, keeps the form of the game while emptying it. Still, the spirit of a game is no free-floating ideal that referees may invoke at will; it can only be read from the contest the rules were built to create, which is why the usual remedy for such an exploit is a better-drafted rule rather than an appeal to conscience.

items.paragraph: Historians divide the past into periods, and the names they choose do more than organise it. To call a thousand years of European history the 'Middle Ages' is to describe them as an interval between two more important times, a long pause between the classical world and its supposed rebirth. Periods are indispensable; without them the past would be an undifferentiated stream. But a period name is never a neutral container. It embeds a view about what mattered, and the historian who uses it without noticing this inherits a verdict rather than reaching one.

items.paragraph: In a market for used cars, sellers know far more about their vehicles than buyers do. items.paragraph: Radio drama is sometimes regarded as a poor relation of film and television, a form that lasted only until pictures could be added. Yet the absence of images is not simply a lack. items.paragraph: Farm soils can store carbon, and practices such as planting cover crops or ploughing less have been shown in many trials to raise the carbon content of the topsoil. This has made soil an attractive climate solution, since farmers can be paid for carbon they lock away. The finding needs careful handling. Gains are often measured only in the upper layers, and some of the apparent increase may be carbon moved from deeper soil rather than newly captured. Soils also reach a new balance after some years and stop accumulating, and the stored carbon can return to the air if the practices are abandoned. Soil carbon is real, but slower, smaller and less secure than a simple accounting suggests.

items.paragraph: In places where many people cycle, the risk of injury for each cyclist tends to be lower than in places where few do. This pattern is often read as proof that drivers become more careful when cyclists are common, so that simply encouraging more cycling will make it safer. The pattern is real, but the causal story may run partly the other way. Cities that have built protected lanes and calmed their traffic attract more cyclists precisely because cycling there is already safer, and more cautious people take up cycling only when it feels safe. Driver adaptation may contribute as well; nobody needs to deny it. What the pattern does not support is the hope that numbers alone, without the infrastructure that draws them, will deliver safety.

items.paragraph: Reviews of film adaptations often turn on fidelity: whether the film kept the plot, the characters and the ending of the book. The criterion is natural but confused. A novel can spend pages inside a character's thoughts, stretch a single moment or move freely across decades; a film must render most of this through image, sound and duration, and a scene transferred unchanged may carry quite different weight on screen. Literal faithfulness can therefore betray what made the book matter, while a film that alters events may preserve it. This does not make every departure justified, and some adaptations change a story for no better reason than convenience. But the question worth asking is whether the film achieves in its own medium something comparable to what the book achieved in its, not whether the two can be matched item by item.
